text: Milo has one hour before he falls into a black hole, and for the next 59 minutes,
he won't feel a thing. Far in the future, Milo is a pilot on a little research ship
orbiting the black hole at the center of our galaxy, 4 million times heavier than the Sunday.
A few minutes ago, his engines fired to adjust his orbit, and they jammed. By the time they
finally died, they had burned away almost all of his sideways speed. And around something this
heavy, if you stop moving sideways, there's only one way left to go. Straight down. No engines,
no way to call for help, just a receiver that can still hear the station,
and an emergency beacon that blinks once every second. He's 180 million kilometers away,
a little farther than the Earth is from the Sunday. That sounds like a lot of room. It isn't. The
seconds. That's how long until Milo falls through the edge of the black hole.
The event horizon. The line that nothing, not even light, ever comes back from. Milo's survival
odds? 12%. Because he isn't alone out here. Not far behind him is the research station, Halo.
And on Halo, watching his signal on a screen, is his sister, Nia. She has one rescue drone,
the fastest machine anyone has ever built. And it has exactly one chance. Nia launches it.
Milo's odds just jumped to 61%. Now here's the first thing that surprises everyone.
Milo is falling toward the heaviest thing in our entire galaxy. And he feels nothing.
No pull, no pressure. He floats in his seat like an astronaut. Because when you fall freely,
gravity is silent. Your body and your ship fall together. And he's lucky in another way.
If this were a small black hole, one just 10 times heavier than the sun, Milo would never make
it to the edge alive. Long before he reached it, the pull on his feet would be so much stronger
than the pull on his head that he'd be stretched thin, like spaghetti. Scientists literally call it
spaghettification. But a giant black hole is gentle at the edge. At the event horizon of
this one, the stretch on Milo's body would be weaker than a fridge magnet.
The monsters are the small ones. Minute 20. The drone is closing in. But Milo is speeding up.
He's now moving at more than 20,000 kilometers every second. And every minute, faster.
Minute 30. Nia's voice comes through the receiver. She's been running the numbers again.
And her voice has changed. Catching up with Milo isn't the problem. The drone will reach
him at minute 47. The problem is what comes next. By then, Milo will be moving at a quarter
of the speed of light. To save him, the drone would have to stop a whole ship moving that fast.
Turn it around and drag it back out. Not even the drone can do that. Not even close.
And now Nia has to make the worst choice of her life. Keep the drone going and lose it too.
Or turn it back. She turns it back. Milo's odds just drop to zero. And he can't even answer her.
Minute 40. And now the sky starts to break. The black hole itself is invisible. It's a hole.
A perfect circle of nothing. But around it, light from the stars behind is being bent.
Warped around the black hole, like the world seen through the bottom of a glass.
Stars that should be hidden appear twice. A whole ring of light wraps around the dark
circle. At minute 59, Milo flies through a place where gravity is so strong,
that light itself can go around in circles. Anyone who could stop and hover right there,
and look straight to the side, could in theory see light that went all the way around the black
hole. They could see the back of their own head. And now, the strangest part of this
whole story. Nia is still watching. On her screen, Milo is slowing down. His ship
drifts closer and closer to the edge. But never quite reaches it. His light gets redder.
Dimmer. His beacon that blinked once every second, blinks slower and slower. Like a heartbeat
running out. To Nia, it looks like her brother is frozen at the edge of the black hole,
fading, but still there. And part of her wants to believe it. He's right there.
He's not even through yet. But that's not what's really happening.
What Nia is seeing is old light. The last light Milo sent out before he crossed,
stretched thinner and thinner as it climbs back out. Milo isn't frozen. For him,
nothing slows down at all. Minute 59 in 30 seconds. Milo crosses the event horizon.
And nothing happens. No wall. No flash. No bump. If he hadn't been watching the clock,
he wouldn't know. But everything has changed. Until now. At least in theory,
a strong enough engine could still have pulled him out. Not anymore. Not with any engine. Not even
light gets out from here. Because inside a black hole, space and time swap places.
The center isn't a place in front of him anymore. It's a moment in his future. As certain as
tomorrow, every direction he could turn, every path he could take, leads to the same moment.
And here is the cruelest twist. If his engines came back on right now,
and he fired them as hard as he could to escape, it would only bring that moment faster.
In here, fighting with everything you've got only makes the end come sooner.
Milo has about 30 seconds left. You may have heard that right now,
he'd look back and watch the entire future of the universe flash by. He doesn't. When he
looks back, he sees the stars, bent and squeezed together. Somewhere among them,
too small to see, is the station. And Nia. The universe is still out there. He just can't ever
get back to it. He never got to say goodbye. So he does the only thing left. He records one
last message for Nia. It will never leave the black hole. Nobody will ever hear it. Then,
in the final fraction of a second, the stretching he escaped at the edge finally catches up with
him. And Milo is gone. Or is he? Stephen Hawking predicted that black holes are not forever.
Very, very slowly, they leak away. This one would take roughly a one followed by 87 zeros
in years. Far longer than the stars will burn. And some physicists think that when a black hole
finally disappears, everything that ever fell in leaves a trace. Scrambled beyond recognition,
but not erased. Not completely. Which means, maybe, somewhere in the last light of a dying
black hole, near the end of time, there's a tiny, unreadable piece of Milo's last message.
Still on its way home, Milo's final survival odds? Zero percent. But his last message?
Might be the one thing a black hole can't keep forever. So let me ask you, if you had one
hour left, and nobody could save you, what would you say in your last message?
And who would you send it to? Tell me in the comments.
